objectives: Master computational + big-data — Bonica DIME ideal points, Grimmer + Stewart text-as-data, social-media analysis.
Survey experiments + RCTs — Gerber + Green, field + lab + online.
Engage AI + democracy + the 2020s — misinformation, recommender amplification, AI-generated content, future of the discipline.

slides.title: Computational + big-data political science: DIME, text-as-data, social media
slides.body:
Political science has been transformed by *digital + computational + big-data* methods over the last 15 years. The subfield-spanning toolkit now includes ideal-point estimation, text-as-data, social-media analysis, network analysis, automated content analysis, + large-scale field experiments.

**Adam Bonica — DIME (Database on Ideology, Money in Politics, and Elections)**. Stanford.
- ***'Mapping the Ideological Marketplace'*** (2014 *AJPS*); ***Avenues of Influence*** (2014); the DIME database — campaign contributions from candidates + donors + PACs, scaled to ideological ideal points (CFscores).
- *Method*: spatial-modeling of contribution networks — donors give to ideologically close candidates; with enough data, candidates + donors can be jointly placed on a continuous ideological scale. Comparable in spirit to DW-NOMINATE (Poole + Rosenthal) for roll-call data, extended to candidates *before* + *outside* legislative voting.
- *Use cases*: measuring primary + general-election candidate ideology; mapping the conservative + liberal donor networks; quantifying asymmetric polarization (cross-ref Hacker + Pierson, lesson 6); identifying ideological drift over candidates' careers.
- *DIME has driven a generation of campaign-finance + polarization research*.

**Justin Grimmer + Brandon Stewart — text-as-data**. Stanford + Princeton.
- ***'Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts'*** (Grimmer + Stewart 2013 *Political Analysis*). Foundational survey paper.
- ***Text as Data: A New Framework for Machine Learning and the Social Sciences*** (Grimmer, Roberts, Stewart 2022, Princeton UP). Comprehensive textbook.
- *Core methods*: tokenization + stopword removal + stemming; bag-of-words + tf-idf; topic models (Latent Dirichlet Allocation — Blei + Ng + Jordan 2003; *Structural Topic Model* — Roberts + Stewart + Tingley 2014); document classification (Naive Bayes, SVM, logistic regression); word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe); contextual embeddings (BERT, RoBERTa, contemporary LLMs); discourse + entity extraction.
- *Applications*: legislative speech analysis (Congress, parliaments); press-release coding; manifesto + party-platform analysis (Comparative Manifesto Project); judicial opinions; news + media-bias measurement; protest event coding.
- *Validation* is the central methodological challenge — automated coding *must* be validated against human gold-standard coding + tested for robustness.
- *Recent: LLM-based methods* — Bisbee + Hopkins; Argyle + Busby + Fulda + Gubler + Rytting + Wingate (2023) *Out of One, Many* (cross-ref lesson 8 sociology + here below); Gilardi + Alizadeh + Kubli (2023 *PNAS*) *ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers for text-annotation tasks*; widespread + controversial adoption of LLMs for political-text annotation.

**James Bisbee — LLMs for political-science research**.
- ***'Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data?'*** (Bisbee et al. 2024 *Political Analysis*) — empirical assessment of LLM-generated 'synthetic samples' as substitutes for human survey data; finds systematic biases + cautions against displacement of human respondents.
- Cross-ref: Argyle et al. 2023 *Political Analysis* — *Out of One, Many*; LLMs prompted with demographic profiles partially replicate ANES patterns + with systematic biases.
- The *silicon samples* + LLM-augmented survey-research debates are central to contemporary methodology (cross-ref lesson 8 sociology + ML risks).

**Social-media analysis**.
- **Pablo Barberá — *'Birds of the Same Feather Tweet Together'*** (2015 *Political Analysis*) — ideal-point estimation from Twitter following behavior. Demonstrated that political ideology can be inferred from social-media network structure.
- **Andy Guess + Brendan Nyhan + Jason Reifler + Joshua Tucker + others — Twitter / X + Facebook misinformation + polarization research**.
- **Sandra González-Bailón — *Decoding the Social World*** (2017); ***The Cascade Effect*** (2024 with Daniel Halpern); social-media diffusion + cascade dynamics + the *exposure paradox*.
- **Joshua Tucker, Andrew Guess, Pablo Barberá, Cristian Vaccari, et al. 2018** — *Fake News, Echo Chambers, and the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election* + survey of the misinformation landscape.
- **The 2023 *Science* + *Nature* Meta election studies** — Guess, Malhotra, Pan, Barberá, Allcott, Brown, Cingel, Crespo-Tenorio, Eckles, Franco, Kennedy, Lazer, Settle, Stroud, Thorson, González-Bailón et al. The largest pre-registered + independently audited study of social-media political effects ever conducted. *Algorithmic ranking, chronological feeds, no-reshares, reduced exposure* treatments tested on Facebook + Instagram users during the 2020 U.S. election. Headline findings: algorithmic ranking + reshares substantially shape *information diet*; effects on political *attitudes + behavior* were smaller than commonly assumed; selective exposure persists across treatments. Methodologically + politically landmark studies.
- **Center for Social Media and Politics (CSMaP, NYU)** — Tucker + Nagler + Bonneau + others.

**Network analysis in political science**.
- **Henry Brady, David Knoke, Mark Granovetter, James Fowler** + the broader political-network literature.
- **Christakis + Fowler — *Connected*** (2009) — social-network effects on voting + political attitudes.
- **Sandra González-Bailón, David Lazer** (next slide) — computational social-network + political diffusion.
- **John Padgett + Walter Powell — *The Emergence of Organizations and Markets*** (2012).

**Computational methods + machine learning in political science**:
- **Political-violence + conflict prediction** — ACLED, GDELT data; ML models for civil-war + protest prediction (cross-ref the *Political Instability Task Force*).
- **Image + video analysis** — Webb Williams + Casas + Wilkerson 2020; Torres + Cantú 2022 — applied to protest event detection + political-ad analysis.
- **Causal-inference machine learning** — *causal forests* (Athey + Imbens), *double ML* (Chernozhukov), *targeted ML* (van der Laan) — for heterogeneous treatment effects in field experiments.
- **Bayesian hierarchical + multilevel regression with poststratification (MRP)** — Gelman + colleagues; small-area opinion estimation.

**Foundational + critical responses**:
- **Lazer et al. 2009 *Science* — 'Computational Social Science'** — manifesto for the field; **Lazer et al. 2020 *Annual Review of Political Science*** update.
- **Salganik *Bit by Bit*** (2018) — methodology textbook.
- **Munger 2019 — *The Limited Value of Non-Replicable Field Experiments in Contexts with Low Implementation Support*** — cautious view of the field-experiment revolution.
- **Critical responses**: digital-divide + sampling-bias critiques; algorithmic-audit + bias-laundering concerns (cross-ref lesson 8 sociology — Benjamin, Eubanks, Noble, O'Neil); platform-research access limits (CrowdTangle shutdown 2024; X API access changes 2023+).

slides.title: Experiments + RCTs: Gerber + Green, field + lab + online
slides.body:
Beginning in the late 1990s + accelerating through the 2010s, political science underwent an *experimental revolution* — laboratory + field + survey + online randomized controlled trials (RCTs) became standard tools for causal inference.

**Alan Gerber + Donald Green — field experiments + GOTV**. Yale.
- ***Get Out the Vote: How to Increase Voter Turnout*** (Green + Gerber 2004, 2008, 2015, 2019). Synthesized 10+ years of GOTV field experiments — door-to-door canvassing, phone calls, mail, social-pressure mailings, robocalls. Door-to-door canvassing remains the most cost-effective per-vote treatment; commercial robocalls have ~null effects; partisan + non-partisan effects differ.
- **Gerber, Green, Larimer (2008 *APSR*) — 'Social Pressure and Voter Turnout: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment'**. Sent voters mailers showing their + neighbors' past voting records (public information). The *social-pressure* treatment boosted turnout by 8.1 percentage points — among the largest experimental effects in political science. *Self-* + *Hawthorne-* effects also boosted turnout.
- ***Field Experiments: Design, Analysis, and Interpretation*** (Gerber + Green 2012). Methodological textbook.
- The *AALPS* / *EGAP* (Experiments in Governance and Politics) network coordinated multi-site experiments globally (Bangladesh, Brazil, India, Kenya, Liberia, Mexico, Sierra Leone, Uganda, ...).
- *Major reviews*: Druckman + Green + Kuklinski + Lupia *Cambridge Handbook of Experimental Political Science* (2011); Mutz *Population-Based Survey Experiments* (2011).

**Lab experiments**:
- **Political-psychology + behavioral-economics labs** — Penn, Stanford, Yale, NYU, MIT, Stony Brook, Northwestern, Berkeley.
- **Lupia + McCubbins — *The Democratic Dilemma*** (1998) — heuristics + reasoning + low-information voting.
- **Sniderman, Brody, Tetlock — *Reasoning and Choice*** (1991).
- **Druckman — framing + ELM (elaboration likelihood model)** in political contexts.
- **Iyengar + Hahn + Krosnick + Walker — selective exposure + media-bias experiments**.
- **Mendelberg — *The Race Card*** (2001) — implicit-racial-appeal lab experiments.
- **Behavioral genetics + neuroscience** — Alford + Funk + Hibbing twin studies; Schreiber + Settle neuro-imaging of political-attitude processing.

**Survey + vignette + conjoint experiments**:
- **Sniderman + Piazza — *The Scar of Race*** (1993) — survey-embedded experiments on racial attitudes.
- **Hainmueller + Hopkins + Yamamoto — 'Causal Inference in Conjoint Analysis'** (2014 *Political Analysis*) — methodology for *conjoint experiments* (respondents choose between multidimensional candidate profiles; multiple causes simultaneously estimated). Now standard in candidate-evaluation + policy-preference research.
- **Bansak + Hainmueller + Hopkins + Yamamoto — conjoint-design + ethical-AI conjoint applications**.
- **Mutz + Mansfield — *Free Trade and the U.S. Public*** (2009-2013); *Population-Based Survey Experiments* (2011).
- **The American National Election Study (ANES)** + the **Cooperative Election Study (CCES, now Cooperative Election Study (CES))** routinely embed experiments.

**Field experiments — major programs**:
- **Vote-mobilization** — Gerber + Green; the *Analyst Institute*; commercial + partisan vote-targeting.
- **Voter persuasion + canvassing** — *Broockman + Kalla 2016 Science 'Durably Reducing Transphobia'* (a deep-canvassing field experiment that found durable attitude change from a 10-minute conversation; subsequent replications + extensions). Major counter-evidence: most persuasion treatments have *small + short-lived* effects (Coppock 2023).
- **Information + accountability** — Banerjee + Duflo style RCTs in development (Esther Duflo + Abhijit Banerjee 2019 Nobel) applied to political accountability — *Bjorkman + Svensson 2009 *QJE* Uganda health-care monitoring*; *Olken 2007 *JPE* Indonesia road-construction audits*; *Pande + Greenstone + Olken 2024+* India pollution monitoring.
- **Voter education + civic information** — varying effects + null findings (Gerber + Green; Adida + Lo + Platas).
- **Online + social-media experiments** — Bond, Fariss, Jones, Kramer, Marlow, Settle, Fowler 2012 *Nature* *A 61-million-person experiment in social influence and political mobilization*; the 2023 Meta election studies (Guess, Malhotra, ... 2023 *Science* + *Nature*).

**Issues + critiques of the experimental revolution**:
- **External validity** — lab + online effects may not generalize to natural-political settings.
- **Publication bias + p-hacking** — pre-registration + registered reports + power-analysis improvements (since ~2013); EGAP + AsPredicted + OSF registries.
- **Spillover + interference** — SUTVA violations; *cluster randomized designs*; *interference-aware estimators* (Aronow + Samii 2017).
- **Ethical issues** — Facebook 2014 *PNAS* emotional-contagion experiment controversy; Catalist + commercial-data-merge concerns; deep-canvassing IRB issues; field-experimental fraud (LaCour-Green 2014 retraction).
- **Critique of the field-experiment revolution** — Heckman *AER* critiques; Munger 2019 limited-value note; *external validity* + scaling concerns.
- **Diversity of participant pools** — most lab + survey experiments still oversample WEIRD + U.S. populations (cross-ref Henrich + Heine + Norenzayan 2010); EGAP + multi-site work has expanded representation.

**The contemporary methodology agenda**: pre-registered + transparently reported experiments; multi-site replication (the *Open Science Collaboration* + *ManyLabs* + the *Psychological Science Accelerator* + political-science analogs — *Time-Sharing Experiments for the Social Sciences (TESS)* + *Many Politics*); causal-inference advances (instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences, synthetic control — Abadie et al.; LATE; double ML); + the combination of experiments with administrative + behavioral + textual data.

slides.title: AI + democracy + the 2020s: misinformation, recommender amplification, AI-generated content, future of the discipline
slides.body:
The 2020s have transformed political science again — generative AI, recommender systems, social-media platforms as institutions, + the algorithmic mediation of public life are now central research objects. The discipline is in flux.

**Misinformation + fake news**.
- **Hunt Allcott + Matthew Gentzkow — 'Social Media and Fake News in the 2016 Election'** (2017 *Journal of Economic Perspectives*). MIT + Stanford. The foundational empirical paper on misinformation in the 2016 U.S. election. Methodology: combined survey data, web-traffic data, + a list of pro-Trump + pro-Clinton fake-news stories. Findings: fake news was *consumed* (~14% of pre-election news diet), but its *effect on vote choice was likely small* — most consumers were already partisans. *Selection*, not persuasion, dominates. Subsequent work: Guess + Nyhan + Reifler 2018 (~10% of voters consumed any fake news; consumers heavily skewed Republican); *Selective Exposure to Misinformation* literature.
- **Andy Guess + Brendan Nyhan + Jason Reifler + colleagues** — multiple landmark papers on misinformation exposure + persistence + corrections.
- **The corrections + backfire-effect literature** — Nyhan + Reifler 2010 (initial *backfire* finding) → Wood + Porter 2019 + others (mostly no backfire on average); corrections somewhat reduce belief without eliminating partisan identity-driven resistance.
- **The Joint Center for Election Sciences + Misinformation reviews** — Lazer et al. 2018 *Science* 'The Science of Fake News'; Tucker et al. 2018 *Social Media, Political Polarization, and Political Disinformation*.
- **2020 + 2024 election cycle research** — Allcott + Braghieri + Eichmeyer + Gentzkow 2020 *AER* on *The Welfare Effects of Social Media* (4-week Facebook deactivation experiment; reduced political polarization + improved well-being); Allcott + Gentzkow + Yu 2019 *Research + Politics* on declining fake-news engagement.
- **Russian + foreign-influence operations** — DiResta + Howard + colleagues; the U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee report on IRA + Russian interference 2018.

**Recommender systems + algorithmic amplification**.
- **The 2023 *Science* + *Nature* Meta election studies** (Guess, Malhotra et al.) — landmark studies on Facebook + Instagram algorithmic ranking + reshares + chronological feeds during the 2020 U.S. election (cross-ref previous slide). Algorithm shapes *information diet*; effects on political *attitudes + behavior* smaller than feared.
- **YouTube recommendation + radicalization** — Munger + Phillips 2022; Hosseinmardi et al. 2021; Chen + Nyhan + Reifler 2022. Initial concerns (Tufekci 2018) about rabbit holes have been substantially nuanced — YouTube radicalization is more *demand-driven* than *recommender-driven*, though policy choices matter.
- **Twitter / X — algorithmic timeline analyses** + the post-Musk-acquisition data shutoff (2023+) that severely curtailed independent research.
- **TikTok + Bytedance — algorithmic feeds for political content**; nascent research; Chinese + global ramifications.

**Yongren Jin + AI-generated political content**.
- Generative AI (GPT-4 + Claude + Gemini + Llama + Mistral) makes it trivial to produce political text, images, video, voice. Research findings: AI-generated political ads can persuade comparably to human-written ones (Goldstein et al. 2024 *PNAS*); AI-generated political images can spread + be believed (Jin et al. — emerging AI-generated political content literature); deepfake audio + video pose specific authentication threats.
- *Major sources of concern*: scale + cost reduction of misinformation production; targeted micro-persuasion; voice + video deepfakes; *chatbots-as-voters* dynamics; *training-data feedback* (LLMs trained on web content increasingly contain AI-generated content + human content).
- **AI + elections — Pippa Norris + Electoral Integrity Project** (lesson 4) on AI-augmented electoral manipulation; **AI Safety Institute reports** on election manipulation risks; **OpenAI + Anthropic + Google policies** on political-content generation + endorsements + election information.
- **Pre-2024-election research** — Sanderson + Goldstein + Park + others mapped vulnerabilities; the *2024 'super-cycle'* (~70 elections globally) was the first large-scale test of generative-AI political content.

**Christopher Bail — affective polarization + social-media interventions**. Duke.
- ***Breaking the Social Media Prism*** (2021). Combined social-network analysis + qualitative interviews + field experiments. Argues social media's *core* dynamics (visibility-seeking, status-driven extreme posting, partisan-bubble reinforcement) create misleading public impressions + intensify identity-based polarization.
- **Bail et al. 2018 *PNAS* — 'Exposure to Opposing Views on Social Media Can Increase Political Polarization'**. Field experiment exposing Republicans + Democrats to out-party Twitter accounts. *Counter-stereotypical exposure* did *not* reduce polarization + sometimes *increased* it — a major challenge to *contact-hypothesis* style interventions on social media (cross-ref Allport 1954; Pettigrew + Tropp 2006).
- **Bail + Polarization Lab Duke** — continued large-scale + experimental work on platform interventions.
- *Implications*: simply exposing people to the other side does not bridge divides; the *form* + *context* of exposure matters; algorithmic + civil-society interventions need careful design + experimental validation.

**AI + democracy — the broader debate**.
- **AI + electoral integrity** — Norris + V-Dem + the Electoral Integrity Project monitor AI-augmented manipulation risks.
- **AI-augmented governance** — chatbots for constituent service, citizen-assembly facilitation, draft-legislation analysis; trial deployments + ethics debates (Landemore *Open Democracy* 2020; Helene Helene + others on AI-supported deliberation).
- **AI-augmented persuasion + microtargeting** — Cambridge Analytica precursor (2018 scandal); current + future generative-AI-augmented microtargeting; *Coppock 2023 Persuasion in Parallel* — most persuasion is small + parallel across audiences (caveats for AI-augmented dynamics).
- **AI risks to democracy** — Acemoglu + Johnson *Power and Progress* (2023) — the political economy of technological-direction choice; LLMs + frontier-AI safety + alignment debates; AI governance (EU AI Act 2024; U.S. executive orders + sectoral regulation).
- **AI + the discipline** — LLMs as research subjects + as research instruments + as text-analysis methods + as 'silicon samples'; the Argyle + Bisbee debates (previous slides); the *replication + transparency + bias-laundering* concerns.

**The discipline's future** — open questions.
- *How does political science study itself* as algorithmically mediated + AI-augmented?
- *Should political science train + curate its own LLMs* on political-text + survey corpora with open access + audit-by-design (cross-ref lesson 8 sociology)?
- *How do classical concepts — power, sovereignty, representation, deliberation, ideology, identity — apply to AI-mediated political life*? Hobbesian sovereignty for AI-governed states? Tocquevillean civil society in algorithmic public spheres? Mills's sociological + Acemoglu + Robinson's institutional analysis of AI capital + power? Rawlsian justice + AI? Mouffe + Brown's critical theory of algorithmic neoliberalism?
- *What does just political-economic transition look like* as AI reshapes labor, governance, education, intimacy, war?
- *Who counts as a political actor + a citizen + a voter* in AI-augmented democracy?

**Closing synthesis**. The discipline began with Plato + Aristotle, was refounded by Hobbes + Locke + Rousseau + Tocqueville, made empirical by Easton + Almond + Verba + Dahl + Lijphart, theoretically deepened by Rawls + Nozick + Walzer + Sandel + Pateman + Mills + Habermas + Mouffe + Brown, comparatively transformed by Acemoglu + Robinson + Tilly + Fukuyama, behaviorally + electorally formalized by Arrow + Downs + Duverger + Achen + Bartels + Bafumi + Herron + Hacker + Pierson + Levitsky + Way + Ziblatt, internationally paradigmed by Morgenthau + Waltz + Mearsheimer + Keohane + Nye + Wendt + Finnemore + Sikkink + Buzan + Booth, politically-economically integrated by Olson + Ostrom + Persson + Tabellini + Hall + Soskice + Piketty, + computationally + AI-mediated through Bonica + Grimmer + Stewart + Bisbee + Gerber + Green + Allcott + Gentzkow + Bail + the contemporary frontier. The classical canon is more relevant than ever; it requires translation + extension to AI capital + algorithmic governance + the digital public sphere. The discipline's future lies in the integration of classical theory + rigorous causal + computational methods + ethical + critical engagement with the AI tools that are now *both* its instruments + its objects of study.

Welcome to 21st-century political science.

question.question: Diagnose AI-generated political content in a contested 2024 election
question.goal: Two days before a contested state election, an AI-generated audio clip purportedly of the incumbent governor admitting electoral fraud goes viral on TikTok + X. Apply the canonical frontier frameworks.

steps.prompt: What does Allcott + Gentzkow + the misinformation literature predict about effects?

acceptedAnswers: exposure can be substantial but effects on vote choice tend to be small because consumers are largely already partisans; selection rather than persuasion dominates

steps.reveal: Allcott + Gentzkow (2017 *JEP*) + Guess + Nyhan + Reifler (2018+): pre-2024 misinformation exposure was substantial (~14% of news diet) but *vote-choice effects* were likely *small* — most consumers were already partisans + already disposed to believe negative claims about the other side (*selection* > *persuasion*). The 2024 generative-AI environment is different in *scale + targeting + production cost* but the basic dynamic may persist. Forecast: *modest* persuasion effects; *substantial* effects on attention + agenda + activation of base; potential *catalyzing* effects on already-undecided voters in close races.

steps.prompt: What does the 2023 Meta election studies + recommender literature predict?

acceptedAnswers: algorithms substantially shape information diet but effects on attitudes and behavior are smaller than feared; reshares and engagement-maximizing ranking can amplify viral content rapidly

hints: Guess et al. 2023 Science + Nature; reshares + algorithmic ranking.
steps.reveal: 2023 Meta election studies (Guess + Malhotra + Pan + Barberá + Allcott + González-Bailón et al. 2023 *Science* + *Nature*): algorithmic ranking + reshares substantially shape *what* users see + how rapidly content spreads; *attitude + behavior* effects from short-term algorithmic interventions were *smaller* than feared. Implication for the AI-audio case: the clip will likely *spread rapidly* through reshares + algorithmic amplification; *attitudinal effects* on partisans likely small; effects on persuadable + low-information voters + on overall *attention* may be larger. Platform moderation lag is a critical variable — pre-fact-check viral periods do most of the damage.

steps.prompt: What does Bail's *Breaking the Social Media Prism* (2021) + Polarization Lab work add?

acceptedAnswers: social media amplifies status-driven extreme content + affective polarization; counter-exposure does not reliably depolarize and can increase polarization; affective dynamics outpace cognitive corrections

steps.reveal: Bail (*Breaking the Social Media Prism* 2021; Bail et al. 2018 *PNAS*): social media's core dynamics — visibility-seeking, status-driven extreme posting, identity reinforcement — *amplify affective polarization*. Counter-stereotypical exposure does *not* reliably depolarize + sometimes *increases* polarization (Bail 2018 *PNAS* — Twitter exposure to out-party accounts). For the AI-audio case: even rapid debunking + corrections may not eliminate the *affective* + *identity-based* reaction; opponents of the governor will integrate the (false) information into their existing partisan schemata. Bail's framework predicts *durable* polarization effects + emphasizes that mere fact-checking is inadequate.

steps.prompt: What policy + research responses follow from Norris electoral-integrity + Allcott + Bail + the AI-democracy debate?

acceptedAnswers: rapid detection and authentication infrastructure, platform pre-bunking + delay + fact-check labels, electoral-integrity audits, civic education, legal accountability for malicious creators, and longitudinal research on AI-content effects

steps.reveal: Responses: (1) *Rapid detection + authentication infrastructure* — content-provenance standards (C2PA, watermarking); deepfake-detection models; cryptographic media provenance. (2) *Platform pre-bunking + delay + labeling* — Hangartner et al. 2022 *PNAS* pre-bunking; Roozenbeek + van der Linden inoculation; rapid labeling + circuit-breakers on viral content (cross-ref Tarleton Gillespie *Custodians of the Internet* 2018, lesson 8 sociology). (3) *Electoral-integrity audits* — Pippa Norris's Electoral Integrity Project + AI-augmented manipulation extensions. (4) *Civic education + media literacy* — Stanford History Education Group; News Literacy Project. (5) *Legal accountability for malicious creators* — defamation law; EU AI Act + Digital Services Act; FEC + state-law AI-disclosure requirements. (6) *Longitudinal + experimental research* — multi-platform + multi-election studies; LLM-generated content fingerprinting + impact measurement (cross-ref Jin AI-generated political content research). Combined technical + institutional + research agenda. None alone suffices.

question.question: Why is Bonica's DIME database transformative for the study of campaign finance + ideology?
options: Bonica (Stanford; *Mapping the Ideological Marketplace* 2014 *AJPS*; *Avenues of Influence* 2014) constructed the *Database on Ideology, Money in Politics, and Elections (DIME)* — campaign contributions from candidates + donors + PACs scaled to ideological ideal points (CFscores). The spatial-modeling method places candidates + donors jointly on a continuous ideological scale, comparable in spirit to Poole + Rosenthal's DW-NOMINATE roll-call data but extended to candidates *before* + *outside* legislative voting + to the underlying donor network. DIME has driven a generation of research on campaign-finance, primary + general-election candidate ideology, donor networks + their effects, ideological drift over candidates' careers, + quantification of *asymmetric polarization* (cross-ref Hacker + Pierson, lesson 6). Bonica's work integrates with DW-NOMINATE (Poole + Rosenthal) + voter ideal-point estimates (Bafumi + Herron, lesson 6) + social-media ideal-point methods (Barberá 2015) to provide a comprehensive multi-source picture of political ideology + the donor + activist + candidate elite shaping U.S. politics.
question.explanation: Bonica's DIME (Stanford; 2014 *AJPS*) constructed campaign-contribution-based ideal points (CFscores) for candidates + donors + PACs. Spatial modeling of contribution networks extends DW-NOMINATE-style ideology measurement to candidates before / outside legislative voting + the donor network. Drove a generation of campaign-finance, polarization, + ideology research; integrates with Bafumi + Herron + Barberá + DW-NOMINATE in modern asymmetric-polarization analysis.

hints: What other ideal-point methods does it integrate with?
slides.workedSolution: Bonica's DIME (2014 *AJPS*) — campaign-contribution ideal points (CFscores) for candidates + donors + PACs; spatial modeling extends DW-NOMINATE beyond roll-call voting + integrates with Bafumi + Herron + Barberá + Poole + Rosenthal in contemporary asymmetric-polarization research.

question.question: Brief a department on a 5-year strategic plan for the AI + computational frontier
question.prompt: Your political-science department is debating a 5-year strategic plan. A faction proposes hiring three FTEs for AI + computational political science (text-as-data + RCT-methods + AI-and-democracy). Another worries this displaces political theory + comparative politics + qualitative methods. Drawing on (a) the Bonica + Grimmer + Stewart + Bisbee + Barberá + González-Bailón frontier; (b) Gerber + Green field experiments; (c) Allcott + Gentzkow + Bail + the AI-democracy literature; + (d) the classical canon from lessons 1-7 (Plato → Aristotle → Hobbes → Tocqueville → Easton → Dahl → Lijphart → Rawls → Mouffe → Brown → Acemoglu + Robinson → Olson → Ostrom → Piketty → Levitsky + Ziblatt), write a ≤220-word memo. Recommend a *both / and* strategy + identify three specific course or hire categories that integrate computational + classical political science rather than substituting one for the other.

question.question: Gerber + Green + Larimer (2008 *APSR*) social-pressure mailing field experiment found turnout of $t_{\text{control}} = 0.297$ in control + $t_{\text{treat}} = 0.378$ in the social-pressure treatment. Compute the absolute treatment effect $\Delta = t_{\text{treat}} - t_{\text{control}}$ as a percentage, rounded to one decimal.
question.hint: $\Delta = 0.378 - 0.297 = 0.081 = 8.1\%$. Gerber + Green + Larimer (2008 *APSR* 'Social Pressure and Voter Turnout') — among the largest experimental effects in political science. The *social-pressure* mailer (showing recipients' + neighbors' past voting records) boosted turnout 8.1 percentage points. *Self-* + *Hawthorne-* effects also boosted turnout in less aggressive variants. Field experiments have since become a standard tool in political science (cross-ref Green + Gerber *Get Out the Vote* 2004, 2008, 2015, 2019).

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, articulate political science's modern frontier by (a) naming one computational + big-data tool + result (Bonica DIME; Grimmer + Stewart + Roberts text-as-data; Bisbee LLM critique; Barberá social-media ideal points; 2023 Meta election studies); (b) one experimental finding (Gerber + Green field experiments; Gerber + Green + Larimer social-pressure 2008 *APSR*; Bail Polarization Lab); (c) one AI-and-democracy finding (Allcott + Gentzkow 2017 misinformation; Bail 2018 *PNAS* exposure-and-polarization; Jin AI-generated content; AI-augmented manipulation + electoral integrity Norris); + (d) one specific risk + one specific opportunity the discipline faces in the next decade.
question.rubric: Mentions: Computational + big-data — Bonica DIME + CFscores (2014); Grimmer + Stewart 2013 + Grimmer + Roberts + Stewart *Text as Data* (2022); Bisbee + Hopkins + Argyle silicon-samples critique; Barberá *Birds of the Same Feather* (2015) social-media ideal points; 2023 Meta election studies (Guess + Malhotra + Pan + Barberá + Allcott + González-Bailón et al. *Science* + *Nature*) — algorithmic ranking + reshares shape information diet, attitude effects smaller than feared; Lazer et al. 2009 + 2020 computational-social-science manifestos. Experiments — Gerber + Green *Get Out the Vote* (2004-2019) + *Field Experiments* (2012); Gerber + Green + Larimer 2008 *APSR* social-pressure 8.1pp effect; Broockman + Kalla 2016 *Science* deep canvassing; conjoint experiments Hainmueller + Hopkins + Yamamoto (2014); the EGAP + multi-site network; the 2020 + 2024 election research. AI + democracy — Allcott + Gentzkow 2017 *JEP* misinformation; Guess + Nyhan + Reifler corrections + exposure; Bail *Breaking the Social Media Prism* (2021) + Bail 2018 *PNAS* exposure does not depolarize + sometimes worsens; Jin + others AI-generated content; Norris *Electoral Integrity Project* + AI manipulation; Acemoglu + Johnson *Power and Progress* (2023). Risks: bias laundering, platform-access shutdowns (CrowdTangle 2024 + X 2023), AI-augmented manipulation, displacement of qualitative + theoretical work, replication + transparency challenges. Opportunities: integrated computational + classical political science; AI-augmented deliberation + assemblies (Landemore *Open Democracy* 2020); new questions for the canon (Hobbes + Tocqueville + Rawls + Mouffe + Acemoglu + Robinson + Piketty applied to algorithmic governance); a discipline that helps shape AI policy. Concludes that political science's future is the integration of classical theory + rigorous methods + AI critique.
